\chapter{Chapter03 — Restrictions}

\section{Overview}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{FABL.Chapter03.Restrictions}.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Indexed sign cube]
\lean{FABL.IndexedSignCube}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p003-b006}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p020-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p023-b004
}
\label{FABL.IndexedSignCube}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign}
For an index type $\iota$, an indexed sign cube is a function assigning a sign in
$\{\pm1\}$ to each element of $\iota$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Indexed monomial]
\lean{FABL.indexedMonomial}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b002}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p022-b001}
\label{FABL.indexedMonomial}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IndexedSignCube, FABL.signValue}
Let $\iota$ be an index type, let $S$ be a finite subset of $\iota$, and let $x$ assign
a sign to each element of $\iota$. The indexed monomial at $x$ is the product, over
$i\in S$, of the real value of the sign assigned to $i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Indexed sign monomial character]
\lean{FABL.indexedSignMonomialChar}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b002}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p022-b004}
\label{FABL.indexedSignMonomialChar}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IndexedSignCube, FABL.indexedMonomial, FABL.signValue}
For an index set $\iota$ and a finite subset $S\subseteq\iota$, the indexed sign
monomial character sends a sign assignment $x\in\{−1,1\}^{\iota}$ to the product of its
signs on the indices in $S$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Injectivity of sign monomials]
\lean{FABL.indexedSignMonomialChar_injective}
\label{FABL.indexedSignMonomialChar_injective}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IndexedSignCube, FABL.indexedMonomial, FABL.indexedSignMonomialChar, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{5}
For any set of indices $\iota$, assign to each finite subset $S\subseteq\iota$ the
character on sign assignments $x\in\{\pm1\}^{\iota}$ given by $x\mapsto\prod_{i\in
S}x_i$. Distinct finite subsets give distinct characters.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Orthogonality of indexed monomials]
\lean{FABL.expect_indexedMonomial_mul}
\proofsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b003}
\label{FABL.expect_indexedMonomial_mul}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IndexedSignCube, FABL.indexedMonomial, FABL.indexedSignMonomialChar, FABL.indexedSignMonomialChar_injective}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\iota$ be a finite set and let $S,T\subseteq\iota$. The uniform expectation over
sign assignments $x:\iota\to\{−1,1\}$ of the product of the monomials indexed by $S$ and
$T$ is $1$ if $S=T$ and $0$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Indexed Walsh basis]
\lean{FABL.indexedWalshBasis}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b003}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p024-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p024-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p024-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p024-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p024-b007,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p025-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p209-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p209-b005
}
\label{FABL.indexedWalshBasis}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IndexedSignCube, FABL.indexedMonomial, FABL.indexedSignMonomialChar, FABL.indexedSignMonomialChar_injective}
For a finite index set $\iota$, the indexed Walsh basis of the real-valued functions on
$\{−1,1\}^{\iota}$ consists of the sign monomials indexed by all subsets
$S\subseteq\iota$. It is a basis over $\mathbb R$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Indexed Fourier coefficient]
\lean{FABL.indexedFourierCoeff}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b003}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p025-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p211-b002
}
\label{FABL.indexedFourierCoeff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IndexedSignCube, FABL.indexedMonomial}
For a finite index set $\iota$, a function $f:\{−1,1\}^{\iota}\to\mathbb R$, and a
finite subset $S\subseteq\iota$, the indexed Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $S$ is the
uniform average over sign assignments $x$ of $f(x)$ times the product of the signs $x_i$
for $i\in S$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Walsh coordinates and Fourier coefficients]
\lean{FABL.indexedWalshBasis_repr_eq_indexedFourierCoeff}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p025-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p025-b005
}
\label{FABL.indexedWalshBasis_repr_eq_indexedFourierCoeff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IndexedSignCube, FABL.expect_indexedMonomial_mul, FABL.indexedFourierCoeff, FABL.indexedMonomial, FABL.indexedWalshBasis}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\iota$ be a finite set, let $f:\{\pm1\}^{\iota}\to\mathbb R$, and let
$T\subseteq\iota$. The $T$-coordinate of $f$ in the Walsh basis is its Fourier
coefficient $\mathbb E_x[f(x)\prod_{i\in T}x_i]$, where the expectation is uniform over
all sign assignments.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
Let $\iota$ be a finite set, let $f:\{\pm1\}^{\iota}\to\mathbb R$, and let
$x\in\{\pm1\}^{\iota}$. Then $f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq\iota}\widehat f(S)\prod_{i\in
S}x_i$, where $\widehat f(S)=\mathbb E_y[f(y)\prod_{i\in S}y_i]$ and the expectation is
uniform over sign assignments.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Empty Fourier coefficient]
\lean{FABL.expect_eq_indexedFourierCoeff_empty}
\proofsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p004-b003}

  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p026-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p026-b007
}
\label{FABL.expect_eq_indexedFourierCoeff_empty}
\leanok

  {FABL.𝔽₂}
  {context}
  {lmn-constant-depth-fourier}

\difficulty{1}
Let $\iota$ be a finite index set and let $f$ be a real-valued function on sign
assignments indexed by $\iota$. The Fourier coefficient of $f$ at the empty set equals
the uniform average of $f$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
Let $\iota$ be a finite set and let $f,g:\{\pm1\}^{\iota}\to\mathbb R$. Then $\mathbb
E_x[f(x)g(x)]=\sum_{S\subseteq\iota}\widehat f(S)\widehat g(S)$, where $\widehat
h(S)=\mathbb E_y[h(y)\prod_{i\in S}y_i]$ and the expectations are uniform over sign
assignments.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{1}
Let $\iota$ be a finite set and let $f:\{\pm1\}^{\iota}\to\mathbb R$. Then $\mathbb
E_x[f(x)^2]=\sum_{S\subseteq\iota}\widehat f(S)^2$, where $\widehat f(S)=\mathbb
E_y[f(y)\prod_{i\in S}y_i]$ and both expectations are uniform over sign assignments.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-cube monomial agreement]
\lean{FABL.indexedMonomial_fin_eq_monomial}
\label{FABL.indexedMonomial_fin_eq_monomial}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.indexedMonomial, FABL.monomial}
\difficulty{1}
For a natural number $n$, a finite set $S$ of coordinates among the $n$ coordinates, and
a sign assignment $x$ on those coordinates, the indexed monomial on $S$ equals the
monomial on the finite sign cube on $n$ coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-cube Fourier coefficient agreement]
\lean{FABL.indexedFourierCoeff_fin_eq_fourierCoeff}
\label{FABL.indexedFourierCoeff_fin_eq_fourierCoeff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.indexedFourierCoeff}
\difficulty{1}
For a natural number $n$, a function $f$ from the sign cube on $n$ coordinates to $\bbr$,
and a set of coordinates $S$, the Fourier coefficient of $f$ defined using indexed sign
assignments equals the coefficient defined using the finite sign cube: both are the
uniform average of $f(x)$ times the product of the signs in $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Indices outside a fixed set]
\lean{FABL.FixedIndex}
\label{FABL.FixedIndex}
\leanok
For a finite index set $\mathrm{Fin}(n)$ and a subset $J\subseteq\mathrm{Fin}(n)$, the
indices outside $J$ are the elements $i\in\mathrm{Fin}(n)$ satisfying $i\notin J$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Sign assignments on a subset]
\lean{FABL.FreeSignCube}
\label{FABL.FreeSignCube}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign}
For a natural number $n$ and a subset $J\subseteq\mathrm{Fin}(n)$, the free sign cube
consists of all assignments of a sign in $\{−1,1\}$ to each index in $J$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Sign assignments outside a subset]
\lean{FABL.FixedSignCube}
\label{FABL.FixedSignCube}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex, FABL.Sign}
For a natural number $n$ and a subset $J\subseteq\mathrm{Fin}(n)$, the fixed sign cube
consists of all assignments of a sign in $\{−1,1\}$ to each index in
$\mathrm{Fin}(n)\setminus J$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Splitting the sign cube by coordinates]
\lean{FABL.signCubeSplitEquiv}
\label{FABL.signCubeSplitEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedSignCube, FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.Sign}
For a natural number $n$ and a subset $J\subseteq\mathrm{Fin}(n)$, the sign cube
$\{−1,1\}^n$ is equivalent to the product of sign assignments on $J$ and sign
assignments on its complement in $\mathrm{Fin}(n)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Recombining sign coordinates]
\lean{FABL.combineSignCube}
\label{FABL.combineSignCube}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedSignCube, FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.signCubeSplitEquiv}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $J$ be a set of coordinates in $\in n$. Given a sign
assignment $y$ on $J$ and a sign assignment $z$ on the coordinates outside $J$, combine
them into the sign vector on all $n$ coordinates that restricts to $y$ on $J$ and to $z$
outside $J$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Free-coordinate recovery]
\lean{FABL.combineSignCube_apply_free}
\label{FABL.combineSignCube_apply_free}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedSignCube, FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.combineSignCube, FABL.signCubeSplitEquiv}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $J$ be a set of indices in $	ext{Fin}(n)$, and let $y$
and $z$ specify signs on the indices in $J$ and outside $J$, respectively. The sign
vector formed by combining $y$ and $z$ agrees with $y$ at every index in $J$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fixed coordinates of a combined sign vector]
\lean{FABL.combineSignCube_apply_fixed}
\label{FABL.combineSignCube_apply_fixed}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex, FABL.FixedSignCube, FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.combineSignCube, FABL.signCubeSplitEquiv}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $J$ be a set of indices in $	ext{Fin}(n)$, let $y$
assign a sign to each index in $J$, and let $z$ assign a sign to each index outside $J$.
If $i$ is an index outside $J$, then the sign vector obtained by combining $y$ and $z$
has value $z(i)$ at $i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Restriction to free coordinates]
\lean{FABL.signRestriction}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p005-b001}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p075-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p098-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p212-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p274-b007
}
\label{FABL.signRestriction}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedSignCube, FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.combineSignCube}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $J\subseteq\mathrm{Fin}(n)$, and let
$f:\{−1,1\}^{\mathrm{Fin}(n)}\to\alpha$ be a function. For each assignment $z$ of signs
outside $J$, the restriction of $f$ at $z$ is the function on sign assignments $y$ in
$J$ obtained by evaluating $f$ on the assignment that agrees with $y$ on $J$ and with
$z$ outside $J$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation of a sign-cube restriction]
\lean{FABL.signRestriction_apply}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p075-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p098-b004
}
\label{FABL.signRestriction_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedSignCube, FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.combineSignCube, FABL.signRestriction}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $J$ be a set of coordinates in the length-$n$ index
set, and let $f$ map sign-valued vectors of length $n$ to a type $\alpha$. For any
assignment $z$ of signs on the coordinates outside $J$ and any assignment $y$ of signs
on $J$, the restriction of $f$ determined by $J$ and $z$, evaluated at $y$, equals $f$
evaluated on the vector formed by combining $y$ and $z$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Lifting a frequency set]
\lean{FABL.liftFreeFrequency}
\label{FABL.liftFreeFrequency}
\leanok
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $J$ be a set of coordinates in $\in n$, and let $S$ be
a set of elements of $J$. The lifted frequency set consists of the corresponding
coordinates in $\in n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Lifting a complementary frequency set]
\lean{FABL.liftFixedFrequency}
\label{FABL.liftFixedFrequency}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $J$ be a set of coordinates in $\in n$, and let $T$ be
a set of coordinates outside $J$. The lifted frequency set consists of those same
coordinates viewed in $\in n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Free part of a frequency set]
\lean{FABL.freeFrequencyPart}
\label{FABL.freeFrequencyPart}
\leanok
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $J$ and $U$ be sets of coordinates in $\in n$. The
free part of $U$ relative to $J$ is the set of elements of $J$ whose underlying
coordinates belong to $U$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Fixed part of a frequency set]
\lean{FABL.fixedFrequencyPart}
\label{FABL.fixedFrequencyPart}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $J$ and $U$ be sets of coordinates in $\in n$. The
fixed part of $U$ relative to $J$ is the set of coordinates outside $J$ whose underlying
coordinates belong to $U$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Membership in the free frequency part]
\lean{FABL.mem_freeFrequencyPart}
\label{FABL.mem_freeFrequencyPart}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.freeFrequencyPart}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, and let $J,U\text{Fin}(n)$ be finite sets. For an element
$i$ of $J$, its corresponding index belongs to the free frequency part exactly when it
belongs to $U$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Membership in the fixed frequency part]
\lean{FABL.mem_fixedFrequencyPart}
\label{FABL.mem_fixedFrequencyPart}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex, FABL.fixedFrequencyPart}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, and let $J,U	ext{Fin}(n)$ be finite sets. For an index
$i	ext{Fin}(n)$ outside $J$, the corresponding element of the fixed frequency part
belongs to that part exactly when $i$ belongs to $U$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Disjoint lifted frequencies]
\lean{FABL.disjoint_liftFreeFrequency_liftFixedFrequency}
\label{FABL.disjoint_liftFreeFrequency_liftFixedFrequency}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex, FABL.liftFixedFrequency, FABL.liftFreeFrequency}
\difficulty{4}
Let $J$ be a subset of the coordinate set $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. For any set $S$ of
coordinates belonging to $J$ and any set $T$ of coordinates outside $J$, their images in
the full coordinate set are disjoint.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Disjoint lifted frequency parts]
\lean{FABL.disjoint_liftFreeFrequencyPart_liftFixedFrequencyPart}
\label{FABL.disjoint_liftFreeFrequencyPart_liftFixedFrequencyPart}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.disjoint_liftFreeFrequency_liftFixedFrequency, FABL.fixedFrequencyPart, FABL.freeFrequencyPart, FABL.liftFixedFrequency, FABL.liftFreeFrequency}
\difficulty{1}
Let $J$ and $U$ be subsets of the coordinate set $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. The frequencies in
$U$ that lie in $J$, lifted to the full coordinate set, are disjoint from the
frequencies in $U$ outside $J$, lifted to the full coordinate set.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Decomposition of a finite index set]
\lean{FABL.liftFreeFrequencyPart_union_liftFixedFrequencyPart}
\label{FABL.liftFreeFrequencyPart_union_liftFixedFrequencyPart}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fixedFrequencyPart, FABL.freeFrequencyPart, FABL.liftFixedFrequency, FABL.liftFreeFrequency}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $J,U$ be subsets of $\in n$. The elements of $U$
lying in $J$, together with those outside $J$, partition $U$; after viewing each part as
a subset of $\in n$, their union is $U$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Unique frequency decomposition]
\lean{FABL.existsUnique_frequency_split}
\label{FABL.existsUnique_frequency_split}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex, FABL.fixedFrequencyPart, FABL.freeFrequencyPart, FABL.liftFixedFrequency, FABL.liftFreeFrequency, FABL.liftFreeFrequencyPart_union_liftFixedFrequencyPart, FABL.mem_fixedFrequencyPart, FABL.mem_freeFrequencyPart}
\difficulty{5}
For finite subsets $J,U\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, there is a unique pair $(S,T)$, with
$S\subseteq J$ and $T$ a finite set of indices outside $J$, such that the union of $S$
and $T$ (viewed as subsets of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$) is $U$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Monomial factorization across a coordinate split]
\lean{FABL.indexedMonomial_lift_union_combine}
\label{FABL.indexedMonomial_lift_union_combine}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex, FABL.FixedSignCube, FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.combineSignCube, FABL.disjoint_liftFreeFrequency_liftFixedFrequency, FABL.indexedMonomial, FABL.liftFixedFrequency, FABL.liftFreeFrequency, FABL.monomial}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $J$ be a set of coordinates in the $n$-dimensional
sign cube. For finite coordinate sets $S$ in $J$ and $T$ outside $J$, and sign
assignments $y$ on $J$ and $z$ outside $J$, the monomial of the full sign assignment
formed from $y$ and $z$, at the union of the lifted sets $S$ and $T$, equals the product
of the monomial of $y$ on $S$ and the monomial of $z$ on $T$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Monomial on the free coordinates]
\lean{FABL.monomial_liftFreeFrequency_combine}
\label{FABL.monomial_liftFreeFrequency_combine}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex, FABL.FixedSignCube, FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.combineSignCube, FABL.indexedMonomial, FABL.indexedMonomial_lift_union_combine, FABL.liftFixedFrequency, FABL.liftFreeFrequency, FABL.monomial}
\difficulty{1}
Let $J$ be a finite set of coordinates among $n$, let $S$ be a finite subset of $J$, and
let $y$ and $z$ be sign assignments on the coordinates in and outside $J$, respectively.
Combine these assignments into an assignment on all $n$ coordinates. The monomial on the
image of $S$ among the original coordinates, evaluated at the combined assignment,
equals the monomial on $S$ evaluated at $y$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Restriction Fourier coefficient]
\lean{FABL.restrictionFourierCoeff}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p007-b002}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p076-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p088-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p098-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p212-b002
}
\label{FABL.restrictionFourierCoeff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedSignCube, FABL.indexedFourierCoeff, FABL.signRestriction}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $J\subseteq\mathrm{Fin}(n)$, and let
$f:\{−1,1\}^{\mathrm{Fin}(n)}\to\mathbb R$. For a subset $S\subseteq J$, the restriction
Fourier coefficient at $S$ is a function of the signs $z$ outside $J$: its value at $z$
is the Fourier coefficient at $S$ of the function obtained by fixing those outside signs
to $z$.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $J$ be a set of coordinates in the $n$-dimensional sign
cube, let $f$ be a real-valued function on that cube, and let $S$ and $T$ be finite sets
of coordinates in $J$ and its complement, respectively. Take the Fourier coefficient
indexed by $T$ of the function of the fixed outside signs whose values are the Fourier
coefficient indexed by $S$ of the restriction of $f$ to the free signs in $J$. This
equals the Fourier coefficient of $f$ indexed by the union of $S$ and $T$, viewed as
coordinate sets in the full cube.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f:\{−1,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}$, let
$J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $S\subseteq J$. Choose uniformly a sign assignment
$z$ on the coordinates outside $J$. The expected Fourier coefficient at $S$ of the
restriction of $f$ obtained by fixing those coordinates to $z$ equals the Fourier
coefficient of $f$ at the frequency $S$, viewed as a subset of all $n$ coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f\colon\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, let
$J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $S\subseteq J$. For each fixed assignment
$z\in\{-1,1\}^{\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus J}$, take the Fourier coefficient of the
restriction of $f$ to the coordinates in $J$, at frequency $S$. The uniform expectation
over $z$ of the square of this coefficient equals the sum, over all subsets $T$ of the
complementary coordinates, of the squared Fourier coefficients of $f$ at frequency
$S\cup T$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Four-coordinate Boolean predicate]
\lean{FABL.example3_19Predicate}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p075-b003}
\label{FABL.example3_19Predicate}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.signValue}
For a sign assignment $x\in\{−1,1\}^{4}$, the predicate holds if either $x_2=x_3=-1$, or
the signs are weakly decreasing in coordinate order, or they are weakly increasing in
coordinate order. Here the two monotonicity conditions use the usual order on
$\{−1,1\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Four-coordinate Boolean function]
\lean{FABL.example3_19Function}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p075-b003}
\label{FABL.example3_19Function}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.example3_19Predicate}
Define a function on sign assignments $x\in\{−1,1\}^{4}$ by assigning $1$ when the
four-coordinate Boolean predicate holds and $-1$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p077-b005,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p078-b002}
\proofstep
  {FABL.affineSubspaceRestriction_apply}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p078-b002}
\difficulty{4}
Let $x=(x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3)\in\{-1,1\}^4$, and let $f(x)$ equal $+1$ if at least one of the
following holds: $x_2=x_3=-1$; $x_0\ge x_1\ge x_2\ge x_3$; or $x_0\le x_1\le x_2\le
x_3$. Otherwise let $f(x)=-1$. Then
\[
f(x)=\frac18-\frac18x_0+\frac18x_1-\frac18x_2-\frac18x_3+\frac38x_0x_1+\frac18x_0x_2-\frac38x_0x_3+\frac38x_1x_2-\frac18x_1x_3+\frac58x_2x_3+\frac18x_0x_1x_2+\frac18x_0x_1x_3-\frac18x_0x_2x_3+\frac18x_1x_2x_3-\frac18x_0x_1x_2x_3.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Example free coordinates]
\lean{FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates}
\label{FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates}
\leanok
The free coordinates in this example are $0$ and $1$ among the four coordinates indexed
by $\in 4$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[First free coordinate]
\lean{FABL.example3_19First}
\label{FABL.example3_19First}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates}
Among the free coordinates $\{0,1\}$ in $\in 4$, the first selected coordinate is $0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A selected free coordinate]
\lean{FABL.example3_19Second}
\label{FABL.example3_19Second}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates}
Among the four coordinates indexed by $\mathrm{Fin}(4)$, the selected free coordinate is
$1$, an element of the set of free coordinates $\{0,1\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Fixed assignment outside two coordinates]
\lean{FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p075-b004}
\label{FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedSignCube, FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates}
Among four coordinates indexed by $\mathrm{Fin}(4)$, let the free coordinates be $0$ and
$1$. On the remaining coordinates, assign sign $1$ at coordinate $2$ and sign $-1$ at
coordinate $3$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Value at the second fixed coordinate]
\lean{FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment_two}
\label{FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment_two}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex, FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment, FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates}
\difficulty{1}
For the fixed sign assignment on the coordinates outside $\{0,1\}$ that assigns $+1$ at
coordinate $2$ and $-1$ at every other such coordinate, its value at coordinate $2$ is
$+1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Value at the third fixed coordinate]
\lean{FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment_three}
\label{FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment_three}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex, FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment, FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates}
\difficulty{1}
For the fixed sign assignment on the coordinates outside $\{0,1\}$ that assigns $+1$ at
coordinate $2$ and $-1$ at every other such coordinate, its value at coordinate $3$ is
$-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Two-bit input from free coordinates]
\lean{FABL.example3_19TwoBitInput}
\label{FABL.example3_19TwoBitInput}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.example3_19First, FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates, FABL.example3_19Second}
For an assignment $y$ of signs to the two free coordinates, form the two-bit sign vector
whose entries are the signs assigned to the first and second free coordinates, in that
order.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[First coordinate of the two-bit input]
\lean{FABL.example3_19TwoBitInput_zero}
\label{FABL.example3_19TwoBitInput_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.example3_19First, FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates, FABL.example3_19TwoBitInput}
\difficulty{1}
Given any assignment of signs to coordinates $0$ and $1$, form the two-bit input whose
entries are those signs in that order. Its coordinate $0$ is the assigned sign at
coordinate $0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Second coordinate of the two-bit input]
\lean{FABL.example3_19TwoBitInput_one}
\label{FABL.example3_19TwoBitInput_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates, FABL.example3_19Second, FABL.example3_19TwoBitInput}
\difficulty{1}
Given any assignment of signs to coordinates $0$ and $1$, form the two-bit input whose
entries are those signs in that order. Its coordinate $1$ (with coordinates numbered
starting at $0$) is the assigned sign at coordinate $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Coordinate preservation under sign-cube combination]
\lean{FABL.combineSignCube_example3_19_zero}
\label{FABL.combineSignCube_example3_19_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.combineSignCube, FABL.combineSignCube_apply_free, FABL.example3_19First, FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment, FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates}
\difficulty{3}
Let the free coordinates in a sign cube of dimension $4$ be $\{0,1\}$, and fix the signs
on the other coordinates by assigning $+1$ at coordinate $2$ and $-1$ at coordinate $3$.
For every assignment $y$ of signs to the free coordinates, combining $y$ with these
fixed signs gives a sign vector whose coordinate $0$ is $y(0)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[A free coordinate is preserved when combining sign assignments]
\lean{FABL.combineSignCube_example3_19_one}
\label{FABL.combineSignCube_example3_19_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.combineSignCube, FABL.combineSignCube_apply_free, FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment, FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates, FABL.example3_19Second}
\difficulty{3}
Let $y$ assign a sign in $\{ -1,1 \}$ to each of the free coordinates $0$ and $1$ in a
four-coordinate sign vector. When $y$ is combined with the fixed assignment that gives
coordinate $2$ the sign $1$ and coordinate $3$ the sign $-1$, the resulting vector has
sign $y(1)$ at coordinate $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[A fixed coordinate of the combined sign vector]
\lean{FABL.combineSignCube_example3_19_two}
\label{FABL.combineSignCube_example3_19_two}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex, FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.combineSignCube, FABL.combineSignCube_apply_fixed, FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment, FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment_two, FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates}
\difficulty{3}
Let $y$ assign a sign in $\{ -1,1\}$ to each of the free coordinates $0$ and $1$.
Combining $y$ with the fixed assignment that gives coordinate $2$ the sign $1$ and
coordinate $3$ the sign $-1$ produces a sign vector whose coordinate $2$ is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Third coordinate of the combined sign vector]
\lean{FABL.combineSignCube_example3_19_three}
\label{FABL.combineSignCube_example3_19_three}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FixedIndex, FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.combineSignCube, FABL.combineSignCube_apply_fixed, FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment, FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment_three, FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates}
\difficulty{3}
For every assignment of signs to coordinates $0$ and $1$, combining it with the fixed
assignment that gives coordinate $2$ the value $1$ and coordinate $3$ the value $-1$
produces a sign vector whose coordinate $3$ is $-1$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
Fix coordinates $2$ and $3$ to $1$ and $−1$, respectively, and let $y$ range over sign
assignments to coordinates $0$ and $1$. The resulting restriction of the four-coordinate
Boolean function equals, at every $y$, the two-bit OR function applied to the signs at
coordinates $0$ and $1$; this OR function is $1$ exactly when both signs are $1$, and is
$−1$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Restriction equals one]
\lean{FABL.example3_19_restriction_eq_one_iff}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p075-b004}
\label{FABL.example3_19_restriction_eq_one_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.example3_19First, FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment, FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates, FABL.example3_19Function, FABL.example3_19Second, FABL.example3_19TwoBitInput, FABL.example3_19_restriction_eq_orFunction, FABL.orFunction, FABL.signRestriction}
\difficulty{3}
Let $y$ assign signs in $\{−1,1\}^2$ to the two free coordinates $0$ and $1$, with
coordinates $2$ and $3$ fixed to $1$ and $−1$, respectively. The restricted Boolean
function takes the value $1$ at $y$ if and only if both free coordinates have value $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier expansion of the restriction]
\lean{FABL.example3_19_restriction_fourier_expansion}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p075-b004}
\label{FABL.example3_19_restriction_fourier_expansion}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.example3_19First, FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment, FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates, FABL.example3_19Function, FABL.example3_19Second, FABL.example3_19TwoBitInput, FABL.example3_19_restriction_eq_orFunction, FABL.orFunction, FABL.signRestriction, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{4}
Fix coordinates $2$ and $3$ to $1$ and $−1$, respectively. For every choice of signs
$y_0,y_1\in\{−1,1\}$ at coordinates $0$ and $1$, the sign-valued restriction of the
four-coordinate Boolean function is $−\frac12+\frac12y_0+\frac12y_1+\frac12y_0y_1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[First coefficient of a restricted Boolean function]
\lean{FABL.example3_19_restrictionFourierCoeff_first}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p075-b004}
\label{FABL.example3_19_restrictionFourierCoeff_first}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.FreeSignCube, FABL.example3_19First, FABL.example3_19FixedAssignment, FABL.example3_19FreeCoordinates, FABL.example3_19Function, FABL.example3_19Second, FABL.example3_19_restriction_fourier_expansion, FABL.expect_indexedMonomial_mul, FABL.indexedFourierCoeff, FABL.indexedMonomial, FABL.restrictionFourierCoeff, FABL.signRestriction, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f:\{-1,1\}^4\to\{-1,1\}$ take value $+1$ precisely when $x_2=x_3=-1$, or when the
four coordinates are weakly decreasing, or when they are weakly increasing; otherwise
let $f(x)=-1$. Restrict $f$ by fixing coordinates $2$ and $3$ to $+1$ and $-1$,
respectively, leaving coordinates $0$ and $1$ free. The Fourier coefficient of this
restricted real-valued function on the singleton coordinate set $\{0\}$ is $\frac12$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Restriction to a linear subspace]
\lean{FABL.subspaceRestriction}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p077-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p197-b009,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p197-b010
}
\label{FABL.subspaceRestriction}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.𝔽₂}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\alpha$ be a type, let
$f:(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n\to\alpha$, and let $H$ be a linear subspace of
$(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n$. The restriction of $f$ to $H$ is the function $H\to\alpha$
that sends each element of $H$ to its value under $f$.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\alpha$ be a type, let $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\alpha$,
let $H$ be a linear subspace of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$, and let $h\in H$. The restriction of
$f$ to $H$, evaluated at $h$, equals $f(h)$, where $h$ on the right is viewed as a
vector in $\mathbb{F}_2^n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Translation of a function's domain]
\lean{FABL.domainTranslate}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p077-b006}
\label{FABL.domainTranslate}
\leanok
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\alpha$ be a type, let
$f:(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n\to\alpha$, and fix $z\in(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n$. The
translated function sends each $x\in(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n$ to $f(x+z)$.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\alpha$ be a type, let $f:(\mathbb F_2)^n\to\alpha$,
and let $z,x\in(\mathbb F_2)^n$. The translate of $f$ by $z$, evaluated at $x$, is
$f(x+z)$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{1}
Let $f\colon\mathbb F_2^n\to\mathbb R$ and let $z,\gamma\in\mathbb F_2^n$. Translating
$f$ by $z$, so that its value at $x$ is $f(x+z)$, multiplies its vector Fourier
coefficient at $\gamma$ by the Walsh character associated with the support of $\gamma$,
evaluated at $z$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{1}
Let $f\colon\mathbb F_2^n\to\mathbb R$ and let $z,\gamma\in\mathbb F_2^n$. The vector
Fourier coefficient of $x\mapsto f(x+z)$ at $\gamma$ equals the original coefficient
multiplied by the binary sign of the dot product of $\gamma$ and $z$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{R}$, and let
$z,x\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$. The value of $f$ translated by $z$ at $x$ is
$\sum_{\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_2^n}\chi_\gamma(z)\,\widehat f(\gamma)\,\chi_\gamma(x)$,
where $\chi_\gamma$ is the Walsh character indexed by $\gamma$ and $\widehat f(\gamma)$
is the corresponding Fourier coefficient.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Restriction to an affine subspace]
\lean{FABL.affineSubspaceRestriction}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p078-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p088-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p197-b009,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p197-b010
}
\label{FABL.affineSubspaceRestriction}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.domainTranslate, FABL.subspaceRestriction, FABL.𝔽₂}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\alpha$ be a type, let
$f:(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n\to\alpha$, let $H$ be a linear subspace of
$(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n$, and fix $z\in(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n$. The function on
$H$ sends each $h\in H$ to $f(h+z)$.
\end{definition}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p077-b005,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p078-b002}
\difficulty{1}
Let $f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\alpha$ be a function, let $H$ be a linear subspace of $\mathbb
F_2^n$, let $z\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and let $h\in H$. The affine subspace restriction of
$f$ at $h$ equals $f(h+z)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Finite-group Fourier coefficient]
\lean{FABL.finiteAddFourierCoeff}
\label{FABL.finiteAddFourierCoeff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.uniformInner}
For a finite abelian group $G$, a real-valued function $g$ on $G$, and a real-valued
additive character $\psi$ on $G$, the finite additive Fourier coefficient of $g$ at
$\psi$ is their inner product with respect to the uniform measure on $G$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Zero Fourier coefficient and expectation]
\lean{FABL.finiteAddFourierCoeff_zero_eq_expect}
\label{FABL.finiteAddFourierCoeff_zero_eq_expect}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.finiteAddFourierCoeff, FABL.uniformInner}
\difficulty{3}
Let $G$ be a finite additive commutative group and let $g:G\to\mathbb{R}$. The Fourier
coefficient of $g$ at the trivial character is its uniform average over $G$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Zero Fourier coefficient as an affine average]

\uses{FABL.affineSubspaceRestriction, FABL.affineSubspaceRestriction_apply, FABL.finiteAddFourierCoeff, FABL.finiteAddFourierCoeff_zero_eq_expect, FABL.𝔽₂}

  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}

\proofstep

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p229-b003,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p229-b004}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f$ be a real-valued function on $\mathbb{F}_2^n$, let
$H$ be a linear subspace of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$, and let $z\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$. The zero
Fourier coefficient of the restriction of $f$ to the affine subspace $H+z$ equals the
uniform average of $f(h+z)$ over $h\in H$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Mean of a Walsh character on a subspace]
\lean{FABL.expect_vectorWalshCharacter_submodule}
\label{FABL.expect_vectorWalshCharacter_submodule}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.perpendicularSubspace, FABL.subspaceEvaluationCharacter, FABL.subspaceEvaluationCharacter_eq_zero_iff, FABL.vectorWalshCharacter, FABL.vectorWalshCharacter_apply, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{4}
Let $H$ be a linear subspace of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and let $\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$.
The average over $h\in H$ of the Walsh character $(-1)^{\sum_{i:\gamma_i\ne 0}h_i}$ is
$1$ if $\gamma$ is orthogonal to every vector in $H$ under the standard dot product over
$\mathbb{F}_2$, and is $0$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

  {direct}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p078-b002}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n\geq0$, let $f:(\mathbb F_2)^n\to\mathbb R$, let $H$ be a linear subspace of
$(\mathbb F_2)^n$, and let $z\in(\mathbb F_2)^n$. The uniform inner product of the
density that is uniform on $H$ with the translate $x\mapsto f(x+z)$ equals
$\sum_{\gamma\in H^\perp}\chi_\gamma(z)\,\widehat f(\gamma)$, where $H^\perp$ is the
orthogonal subspace for the standard dot product, $\chi_\gamma$ is the corresponding
Walsh character, and $\widehat f(\gamma)$ is the Fourier coefficient of $f$.
\end{theorem}

  {FABL.expect_vectorWalshCharacter_submodule}
  {direct}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p072-b004}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{R}$, let $H$ be a
linear subspace of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$, and let $z\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$. The uniform average
of $f(h+z)$ over $h\in H$ equals $\sum_{\gamma\in H^\perp}\chi_\gamma(z)\widehat
f(\operatorname{supp}\gamma)$, where $H^\perp$ is the orthogonal subspace, $\chi_\gamma$
is the Walsh character indexed by $\gamma$, and $\widehat f(U)$ is the Fourier
coefficient indexed by $U\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Affine restriction and uniform inner product]
\lean{FABL.expect_affineSubspaceRestriction_eq_uniformInner}
\label{FABL.expect_affineSubspaceRestriction_eq_uniformInner}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.affineSubspaceRestriction, FABL.domainTranslate, FABL.expect_affineSubspaceRestriction_eq_sum, FABL.subsetDensity, FABL.uniformInner_subsetDensity_domainTranslate_eq_sum, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{R}$, let $H$ be a
linear subspace of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$, and let $z\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$. The uniform average
of $f(h+z)$ over $h\in H$ equals the uniform inner product of the density of $H$ with
the function $x\mapsto f(x+z)$ on $\mathbb{F}_2^n$.
\end{theorem}
